01.note: A man on his deathbed wrote a bill of divorce for his wife as Shabbat was approaching, but did not manage to hand it to her, and the next day his condition grew worse. People came to Rava, who told them: have him transfer to her the spot where the document is lying, and let her close and open the door there to take possession of it, and the document with it. Rav Ilish objected that whatever a wife acquires belongs to her husband, and Rava was embarrassed. In the end it emerged that she was only betrothed, not married. Rava said the rule about a married woman would not apply to a betrothed one, and then ruled that for either kind of wife, her bill of divorce and her courtyard reach her at the same moment.
01.why: The discussion is about whether a woman's own courtyard can receive her bill of divorce, given her husband's rights in her property. The Gemara then says Rava first stated his principle that the divorce and the courtyard arrive together in connection with this incident.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage asked what to do; his ruling is challenged and he then restates it.

people.name: Rav Ilish
people.about: Challenges Rava, pointing out that what a wife acquires belongs to her husband.

terms.meaning: The document (a get) a husband gives his wife to end the marriage. The divorce takes effect when it reaches her hand or her property.
A woman in the first stage of Jewish marriage: legally bound to her husband but not yet living with him as his wife.
A formal act, such as locking, fencing or breaching a wall, by which a person acquires land. The mishna quoted lists these.

02.note: A man threw a bill of divorce to his wife while she was standing in a courtyard, and it landed on a wooden board. Rav Yosef said they must look at the board's size: if it measured four cubits by four cubits it counts as a separate area of its own, and she is not divorced; if it was smaller, it is all one area with the courtyard, and she is divorced.
02.why: The Gemara has been asking how a courtyard can receive a bill of divorce for a woman. It then works out that the case must be one where the husband lent her his courtyard, since a loan covers one area, not a second one.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who rules on where the bill of divorce landed.

terms.meaning: The document (a get) a husband gives his wife to end the marriage; it takes effect when it reaches her hand or a place that acquires for her.
A measure of length, roughly the distance from elbow to fingertip. Four cubits by four is the size at which an area counts as a place of its own.
An area treated as a single place in law. Whether the board is its own domain or part of the courtyard decides whether the document reached her.

03.note: After Rabbi Eliezer died, four Sages came forward to refute his ruling on a divorce that leaves the woman free to marry anyone except one named man. Rabbi Tarfon argued that such a divorce could cancel a Torah law, the duty of levirate marriage. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili said that what is forbidden is forbidden to everyone. Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya said a document of severance must sever the bond completely. Rabbi Akiva argued that it could void the divorce and make her later children mamzerim, and that she would count as a widow to one priest and a divorcee to everyone else. Each ended: this is not severance. Rabbi Yehoshua told them that one does not refute a lion after his death.
03.why: The Gemara has been exploring a husband's stipulation that forbids his ex-wife one man. Afterward Rava says every one of these refutations can itself be answered except Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's, and the Gemara goes through them one by one.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage, now dead, whose ruling the others set out to refute.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: Argues the stipulation could uproot the law of levirate marriage.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: Argues from the Torah's word for divorce, severance.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Gives two arguments: void divorces and children who would be mamzerim, and the case of a priest.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Tells the others not to refute a great Sage who can no longer answer.

terms.meaning: When a man dies childless, his brother marries the widow. A stipulation forbidding her to that brother would block this Torah duty.
The Torah calls a bill of divorce a scroll of severance; the argument is that it must cut every tie between husband and wife.
Plural of mamzer: a child born of a forbidden union such as adultery, who is barred from marrying most Jews.
An argument from a lighter case to a weightier one: if the lesser prohibition applies, the greater one surely does.

04.note: A rumor spread that a certain woman had been betrothed to a Torah student. Rav Hama summoned her father and asked him exactly what had happened. The father said the student had betrothed her on condition that he would not go to Bei Hozai, and then he went, so the betrothal was void. Rav Hama answered that since this explanation did not exist when the rumor spread, the father could not now create it, and the rumor had to be taken seriously.
04.why: Abaye and Rav Yosef have just argued over whether a court sets aside an unconfirmed rumor that a woman is betrothed; Rav Yosef says places differ. This is the first of several such cases the Gemara brings, and here the rumor is not set aside.

people.name: Rav Ḥama
people.about: The Sage who questions the woman's father and rules on the rumor.

terms.meaning: Betrothal is the first, legally binding stage of Jewish marriage. A rumor that a woman is betrothed could stop her marrying anyone else.
A betrothal made on a stated condition; if the condition is broken, the betrothal never took effect.

05.note: A rumor spread that a certain woman had been betrothed with a mat of dates from the spring of Bei Shifei. Rav Idi bar Avin sent the case to Abaye, asking what to do. Abaye answered that even those who say a rumor is not set aside would set this one aside: if she marries someone else, people will not slander her, but will say the Sages looked into the betrothal and found the mat was not worth a peruta.
05.why: The Gemara is debating whether a court sets aside a rumor that a woman is betrothed, and brings a series of cases. This one shows Abaye making an exception even under the strict view, because the rumor itself points to an invalid betrothal.

people.name: Rav Idi bar Avin
people.about: Sends the case to Abaye for a ruling.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Rules that this rumor is set aside.

terms.meaning: The smallest coin. A betrothal must be made with something worth at least a peruta, or it does not take effect.
To disregard a rumor that a woman is betrothed, so that she may marry someone else.

06.note: A rumor spread that a certain woman had been betrothed to a boy who was still a minor but looked like an adult. Rav Mordekhai told Rav Ashi there had already been such a case, and the Sages said the boy had not yet reached the divisions of Reuben, a phrase from the book of Judges about maturity of heart, so the betrothal counted for nothing.
06.why: This closes the Gemara's series of cases on whether a rumor of betrothal is set aside. The Gemara then turns to the mishna's rule that a rumor counts only when there is no explanation for it.

people.name: Rav Mordekhai
people.about: Tells Rav Ashi of an earlier case like this one.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage to whom the precedent is reported.

terms.meaning: A child below the age of legal adulthood. A minor boy cannot make a valid betrothal, however grown he looks.
Words from Judges 5:16, read here to mean the maturity of mind that comes with adulthood.

07.note: When Shammai the Elder's daughter-in-law gave birth to a son, Shammai broke away the plaster of the ceiling and laid sukka covering over the bed, for the baby's sake. Mar Zutra cites this as proof that Shammai's school acted on its own rulings. The Gemara answers that it proves nothing: anyone watching would think he did it only to let in more air.
07.why: The Gemara is asking whether Beit Shammai actually put their rulings into practice where they differed from Beit Hillel. This incident is offered as evidence that they did, and the Gemara deflects it.

people.name: Shammai the Elder
people.about: Makes a sukka over the bed of his newborn grandson.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: Cites the incident as an objection in the discussion.

terms.meaning: The temporary booth Jews dwell in during the festival of Sukkot. Its roof must be made of plant covering, not plaster.
The school of the Sage Shammai, which often disagreed with the school of Hillel (Beit Hillel). The law usually follows Beit Hillel.

08.note: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok recalled studying with Rabbi Yohanan the Horani and seeing him eat dry bread with salt in years of drought. He told his father, who had him bring olives. Rabbi Yohanan saw they were moist and said only, I do not eat olives; the translation explains he feared they had become ritually impure. Told again, the father sent word that the barrel had been pierced but the hole was clogged by sediment, a case even Beit Hillel rule pure. Though Rabbi Yohanan was a disciple of Shammai, he always acted by Beit Hillel's rulings.
08.why: The Gemara is gathering evidence on whether Beit Shammai acted on their own rulings. It argues that praising Rabbi Yohanan for following Beit Hillel makes sense only if Shammai's disciples normally followed Shammai.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok
people.about: Tells the story of his teacher; carries the olives and messages between him and his father.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan the Ḥorani
people.about: Rabbi Elazar's teacher, a disciple of Shammai who acted by Beit Hillel's rulings.

terms.meaning: A state, under biblical law, that forbids certain foods to those who keep strict purity. Food can become liable to it once moistened by certain liquids.
The schools of the Sages Shammai and Hillel, which disagreed on many laws, including whether olive juice makes olives liable to impurity.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

09.note: A ruling permitting the rival wife of a daughter was said in the name of Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas, a great but very old Sage who could no longer come to the study hall. Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and Rabbi Akiva went to him. He seated each on a golden couch, blessing the young Elazar and greeting Akiva as famous. When they asked, he said the law follows Beit Hillel; the ruling came from his younger brother Yonatan, a sharp disciple of Shammai, the firstborn of the Satan. He swore that the prophet Haggai, sitting on that very mortar, had forbidden the rival wife. Leaving, Akiva met Yonatan and withstood all his objections; Yonatan sneered that he was not yet even a cattle herder, and Akiva answered: not even a shepherd.
09.why: The Gemara had quoted only the opening line, as evidence that Beit Shammai's view was once followed in practice; here it tells the whole incident. Afterward it explains Haggai's other two rulings.

people.name: Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas
people.about: A great, aged Sage with dimmed eyes; the ruling was wrongly credited to him.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Volunteers to go to Rabbi Dosa and introduces his companions.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: Son of Rabbi Dosa's colleague Azarya; Rabbi Dosa blesses him with a verse.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Famous Sage; withstands Yonatan's objections and answers his insult humbly.

people.name: Yonatan
people.about: Rabbi Dosa's younger brother, a disciple of Shammai, who permitted the rival wife.

terms.meaning: When a man dies childless, his brother normally marries a widow. If one widow is that brother's own daughter she is forbidden to him; the question is whether her co-wife is also freed. Beit Shammai permit her to the brothers.
The schools of the Sages Shammai and Hillel, which disagreed on many laws. The law usually follows Beit Hillel.
An insult-compliment: someone extremely sharp and brazen in argument.

10.note: Rav Hisda recalled hearing from a great man, Rabbi Ami, that the Sages forbade a daughter-in-law only because of a daughter-in-law, and not understanding it. Chaldean astrologers had told him he would be a teacher. He said to himself: if I become a great teacher, I will work it out on my own; if I become a teacher of children, I will ask the Sages who come to the synagogue. Now, he said, he had worked it out himself: a man's daughter's daughter-in-law was forbidden only because she could be confused with his son's daughter-in-law.
10.why: The Gemara is listing relatives forbidden by the Sages rather than by the Torah, and has just corrected one item on Rav's list to read his daughter's daughter-in-law. Rav Hisda's account supplies the reason for that prohibition.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Tells how he came to understand a teaching he heard from Rabbi Ami.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: The great man whose short teaching Rav Hisda heard.

terms.meaning: Astrologers who foretold a person's future; here they predict Rav Hisda will become a teacher.
Relatives one may not marry. Some are forbidden by the Torah; the Sages added others so that people would not confuse them with the Torah's cases.

11.note: Rabbi Yehuda was told of an armed bandit who was being led out to be executed at the pass of Cappadocia. He told the people there: go and tell the wife of Shimon the Priest that I killed her husband as I entered Lod (some say: as he entered Lod). On that word, his wife was allowed to remarry. Rabbi Yehuda replied that this proved nothing, because the bandit had said: I was with his murderers.
11.why: The mishna lets a woman remarry on a witness who says I killed him, while Rabbi Yehuda accepts only we killed him, which Rav Yehuda reads as I was with his murderers. This teaching is the basis for that distinction; the Gemara then explains how a mere accomplice was executed.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who is told of the case and reads it his own way.

people.name: Shimon the Priest
people.about: The man the bandit said was killed; his wife was allowed to remarry.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.
A woman whose husband disappears may not remarry until his death is established; here the bandit's words were accepted as that evidence.

12.note: Ravin brought Rabbi Yohanan's teaching that a woman who waits ten years after her husband before marrying again can no longer bear children; Rav Nahman said this applies only if she did not intend to remarry. Rava told his wife, the daughter of Rav Hisda, that the Sages were gossiping about her, since, as the translation explains, she had borne him children after more than ten years without a husband. She answered: My mind was on you.
12.why: The Gemara has been discussing sexual relations that cannot lead to pregnancy; it moves to this teaching about when a woman can still conceive, and Rava's exchange shows Rav Nahman's limit on it.

people.name: Ravin
people.about: Brings Rabbi Yohanan's teaching from the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The Sage whose teaching about ten years Ravin reports.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Limits the teaching to a woman who did not intend to remarry.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Tells his wife that the Sages are gossiping about her.

people.name: daughter of Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Rava's wife, who answers that her mind was on him.

13.note: A woman came to Rav Yosef and told him that she had waited ten years after her husband and still given birth. He told her: My daughter, do not cast aspersions on the words of the Sages. She then admitted to him that she had had relations with a gentile.
13.why: Rabbi Yohanan has taught that a woman who waits ten years after her husband before remarrying can no longer conceive. The woman's case looks like a challenge to that teaching, and her confession shows it is not one.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage the woman comes to, who defends the Sages' teaching.

terms.meaning: A non-Jew.

14.note: When Rav came to Dardeshir, he publicly announced: Who will be my wife for the day? Rav Nahman made the same announcement when he came to Shakhnetziv. The Gemara answers that Sages are different, since their names are famous and their children will always be known. It also explains how they could marry on arrival: they sent messengers ahead so the woman could count seven clean days, or else they only spent time alone with her, since, as the saying goes, one who has bread in his basket is not like one who has none.
14.why: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov has just taught that a man should not marry wives in two countries, lest his children meet and unknowingly marry each other. The Gemara cites these two Sages' conduct as a challenge to that teaching.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who, visiting Dardeshir, announced he was seeking a wife for his stay.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: A Sage who did the same when visiting Shakhnetziv.

terms.meaning: After possible menstrual bleeding, a woman counts seven days without bleeding and immerses in a ritual bath before marital relations are permitted.
Being alone together with a woman. Here the Gemara suggests the Sages married only for companionship, not relations.

15.note: Rabbi Aha, lord of the capital, and Rabbi Tanhum son of Rabbi Hiyya of Akko village ransomed captive women who had been brought from Armon to Tiberias. One of them had been made pregnant by a gentile. They came to Rabbi Ami to ask about the child, and he told them that Rabbi Yohanan, Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Hanina all say that the child of a gentile or a slave and a Jewish woman is a mamzer.
15.why: The Gemara is debating the status of a child born to a Jewish woman and a gentile or slave. Rav Yosef then answers that counting names proves nothing, and lists Sages who rule such a child of unflawed lineage.

people.name: Rabbi Aḥa
people.about: Called lord of the capital; one of the two who ransomed the captives.

people.name: Rabbi Tanḥum
people.about: Son of Rabbi Hiyya, of Akko village; the other ransomer.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: The Sage they ask, who cites three Sages' ruling.

terms.meaning: A child born of a forbidden union, barred from marrying most Jews. The question is whether a gentile father makes a child a mamzer.
Paid ransom to free Jews taken captive, a high duty in Jewish law.

16.note: A man came to Rav and asked about the child of a gentile or slave and a Jewish woman. Rav said the child's lineage is unflawed. The man, himself such a child, said: then give me your daughter. Rav refused. His grandson Shimi bar Hiyya quoted a saying about a camel that supposedly dances in Medes but does not when put to the test. Rav said that even if the man were like Joshua son of Nun he would not give him his daughter. Shimi answered that others would marry their daughters to a Joshua, but if Rav refused this man, no one would. The man would not leave and kept pleading. Rav set his eyes on him, and he died.
16.why: Abaye has argued that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi permits such a child to marry within Israel. The Gemara brings this incident to show Rav ruled the same way, then lists other Sages who did too.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Rules the child's lineage unflawed but refuses to give the man his daughter.

people.name: Shimi bar Ḥiyya
people.about: Rav's grandson, who challenges Rav's refusal.

terms.meaning: A small measure of volume. The proverb's camel dances on a space holding a single kav.
Free of any bar on marrying within the Jewish community.

17.note: Beloreya was a woman converting to Judaism. Her slaves immersed before she did, and the case came before the Sages, who ruled that the slaves had acquired themselves and were free.
17.why: Rav has ruled that a slave bought from a gentile who immerses for conversion before his new Jewish owner immerses him goes free. Rav Hisda infers from this case that had they immersed after her they would not have gone free, and raises it as a challenge; Rava answers it.

people.name: Beloreya
people.about: A convert whose slaves immersed before her.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Raises the incident as an objection in the discussion.

terms.meaning: Immersion in a ritual bath is a required step in converting to Judaism, and also in a gentile slave entering a Jewish owner's service.
A person who has formally joined the Jewish people.

18.note: When Rav Ashi wanted to immerse his slave Minyamin, he handed him over to Ravina and Rav Aha son of Rava and told them he would hold them responsible for him. They put a bridle on Minyamin's neck; at the moment of immersion they loosened it, and then tightened it again.
18.why: Shmuel has just said an owner must hold his slave firmly in the water, so that the immersion counts as entering slavery rather than conversion to freedom. This incident shows how it was done; the Gemara then explains each step.

people.name: Minyamin
people.about: Rav Ashi's slave, who is being immersed.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Minyamin's owner, who hands him to two Sages for the immersion.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: One of the two Sages who perform the immersion.

people.name: Rav Aḥa, son of Rava
people.about: The other Sage who performs the immersion.

terms.meaning: A gentile slave acquired by a Jew is immersed in a ritual bath. If the slave declares it is for conversion as a free man, he goes free.
A strap placed on the slave's neck to show the owner's control during the immersion.

18.flag: The STORY stops mid-incident: the next segment (the bucket of clay placed on Minyamin's head after immersion) belongs to the same incident.

19.note: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba came to Gavla. He saw Jewish women pregnant by converts who had been circumcised but not immersed, Jews drinking their wine that gentiles had poured, and Jews eating lupines that gentiles had cooked, and he said nothing to them. When he came to Rabbi Yohanan, Rabbi Yohanan told him to go and declare their children mamzerim, their wine forbidden as libation wine, and their lupines forbidden as food cooked by gentiles, because they were not learned in Torah.
19.why: The Gemara has been discussing immersion as the step that completes a conversion. Afterward it shows Rabbi Yohanan's ruling follows his own views: no one is a convert until circumcised and immersed, and a gentile's child with a Jewish woman is a mamzer.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba
people.about: Visits Gavla, sees lax practice and says nothing, then reports it.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Tells him to make public declarations against these practices.

terms.meaning: Plural of mamzer: a child of a forbidden union, barred from marrying most Jews.
Wine poured as an offering to idols, forbidden to Jews. The Sages extended the ban to wine handled by gentiles.
A rabbinic ban on certain foods cooked by non-Jews, even if the ingredients are permitted.
Bitter beans that must be cooked before eating.

20.note: Rabba told of an incident in the house of Rabbi Hiyya bar Rabbi. In Rav Yosef's version Rabbi Oshaya bar Rabbi was also there, and in Rav Safra's version Rabbi Oshaya son of Rabbi Hiyya as well. A convert came who had been circumcised but not yet immersed, and he was told: stay here until tomorrow, and we will immerse you.
20.why: The Gemara has been debating whether circumcision or immersion completes a conversion. Rabba then draws three rules from this incident: a conversion needs a court of three, it needs both circumcision and immersion, and a convert is not immersed at night.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Reports the incident and draws rules from it.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Rabbi
people.about: In whose house the convert came.

people.name: Rabbi Oshaya bar Rabbi
people.about: Present, in the version Rav Yosef teaches.

people.name: Rabbi Oshaya, son of Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Also present, in the version Rav Safra teaches.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: Teaches the version with three Sages present.

terms.meaning: A person joining the Jewish people. For a man this requires circumcision and immersion in a ritual bath.
Dip fully in a ritual bath, the final step of conversion.
